name: ctbignum
workload: Fixed-width multiplication of 2, 4 and 8 64-bit-limb integers (100-500 bit range), run time and compile time.
claimed_speedup: 2 limbs: 4 ns vs GMP 14 ns (3.5x); 4 limbs: 18 ns vs 29 ns (1.6x); 8 limbs: 85 ns vs GMP 67 ns (GMP 1.3x faster)
hardware: 2017 MacBook Pro, quad-core 2.3 GHz Intel Core i5 (Kaby Lake), 16 GB, Turbo Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Fixed-width only (sizes known at compile time), C++20 header-only; wins only for small limb counts via inlining and unrolling.
caveats: GMP is faster at 8 limbs; numbers from the 2018 paper on 2017 hardware; benchmark code is in the repo (needs GMP, NTL, libff, Google Benchmark) but I did not open the benchmark directory itself.
found_via: WebSearch result Multiprecision Arithmetic for Cryptology in C++ (arXiv 1804.07236)
WebSearch: intx uint256 C++ fixed width big integer faster than GMP benchmark -> arXiv 1804.07236

name: Truncated batch SIMD AVX512 Montgomery multiplication
workload: Batch Montgomery multiplication and fixed-window modular exponentiation, 260-4154 bit operands using AVX512 VPMADD52
claimed_speedup: Montgomery multiplication 5.34x (1024-bit) to 3.95x (4096-bit) vs GMP; fixed-window exponentiation 5.42x to 4.66x vs GMP; vs OpenSSL 3.69-4.31x
hardware: Dell Inspiron laptop, 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @ 2.80GHz, Turbo Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Needs AVX512-IFMA; batch (SIMD across independent operands) not single-operation latency.
caveats: Batch throughput compared with per-operation GMP; results are for modular arithmetic, not general bigint; last commit not checked; benchmark code assumed public in repo (README not read in full).
found_via: WebSearch: arXiv big integer multiplication outperforms GMP AVX-512 IFMA

name: Arb
workload: Arbitrary-precision dot product and matrix multiplication at 53-212+ bit precision (Table I, cycles per term).
claimed_speedup: about twice as fast as MPFR at several hundred bits, 3-4 times up to 128 bits; Table I: 212 bits 133 vs 208 cycles/term, 106 bits 49 vs 156, 53 bits 40 vs 99
tradeoffs: Ball (midpoint-radius interval) arithmetic, so not a drop-in MPFR replacement; carries error bounds.
caveats: Repo is archived because Arb was merged into FLINT; use FLINT for current code. Compiler flags unstated in the paper; measured with GMP 6.1 and MPFR 4.0 in Dec 2018. Repo README also gives a hypergeometric table vs MPFR, which I did not use. Same code now lives in FLINT, so consider folding into the FLINT entry.
found_via: WebSearch: Arb ball arithmetic faster than MPFR benchmark
WebSearch: FLINT fmpz arb arbitrary-precision ball arithmetic faster than MPFR benchmark

name: midint-arithmetic-division (GPU multi-precision division)
workload: Batched shifted-inverse integer division on GPU for 2^13 to 2^18-bit operands
claimed_speedup: 11.3x faster than GMP at 2^18 bits; 14.0x at 2^17; 18.9x at 2^16; 12.6x at 2^15; 7.4x at 2^14; 11.1x at 2^13
tradeoffs: Requires NVIDIA GPU; batched workloads; CUDA/Futhark.
caveats: Repo is a fork of coancea/midint-arithmetic (parent URL not opened); license not found; GPU vs CPU GMP comparison; README says it does not beat CGBN in its range; uses CUDA so not a plain C++ library.
found_via: WebSearch: GPU CUDA multiple precision integer arithmetic library faster than GMP

name: DigitsOnTurbo (DoT)
workload: Large-number addition, subtraction, multiplication with x86 SIMD intrinsics, plus pi computation
claimed_speedup: addition/subtraction up to 3.81x geometric mean; multiplication up to 1.41x geometric mean; pi computation up to 19.3%; multiplication of larger operands up to 48.7%
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6548Y+ (Emerald Rapids) and Xeon Max 9462 (Sapphire Rapids)
tradeoffs: 1,013 lines of portable C with intrinsics; integrates into GMP and OpenSSL with ~40 lines of changes.
caveats: Code only at an anonymous review URL (anonymous.4open.science/r/DigitsOnTurbo, not opened); no license found; preprint not peer-reviewed; geometric-mean figures are for best cases.
found_via: WebSearch: arXiv big integer multiplication outperforms GMP AVX-512 IFMA

name: FLINT
workload: 100 million digits of pi; 100x100 integer matrix multiplication at 10/100/1000-bit entries
claimed_speedup: pi: GMP 62.1 s vs FLINT 31.6 s single-thread (about 2x) and 9.34 s on 8 threads (6.6x, derived from page data); 100x100 matmul 10-bit entries 0.0122 s vs 0.00395 s naive, optimised 8-thread 0.0000675 s
tradeoffs: Uses GMP/MPIR underneath; FLINT 3 absorbs Arb, Calcium; fft_small is AVX2/NEON tuned.
caveats: First-party; compiler/flags not given; FLINT naive matmul is not faster than GMP at 100/1000 bits; github issue 2852 reports fft_small slower than GMP on a Zen 5 EPYC (not opened).
found_via: WebSearch: FLINT fmpz arb arbitrary-precision ball arithmetic faster than MPFR benchmark
WebSearch: FLINT fmpz arithmetic faster than GMP benchmark

name: mp++
workload: 1-limb unsigned integer dot product, vector multiply-add and vector division over small operands (also compared with Boost.Multiprecision cpp_int/gmp_int and FLINT fmpzxx).
claimed_speedup: dot product: almost 4 times faster than GMP; multiply-add: more than 7 times faster; division: about 8 times faster (mp++ and FLINT)
tradeoffs: C++ wrapper built on GMP/MPFR/MPC; small-value optimisation (inline limbs) beats GMP only for small operands.
caveats: Docs state no compiler, flags or CPU. Advantage is limited to 1-limb values; large operands defer to GMP.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ big integer arbitrary precision library faster than GMP benchmark github
WebSearch: multiprecision integer arithmetic library faster than GMP benchmark C++ github

tradeoffs: Requires AES-NI (Intel/AMD/POWER); 2048-bit state; main selling point is cryptographic-strength backtracking resistance at near-PCG speed, not raw speed

name: Randen
workload: Microbenchmark and applied tasks (Fisher-Yates shuffle, reservoir sampling, Monte Carlo) for an AES-NI based backtracking-resistant generator
claimed_speedup: README: 1.54 cycles/byte microbenchmark between pcg64_c32 (0.78) and mt19937_64 (1.79); reservoir sampling 2.60 cycles/byte slightly ahead of competitors. Paper: 1.1x faster than Mersenne Twister (geometric mean) in applied tasks; PCG similar or faster in applied tasks; microbenchmark shows PCG slightly ahead
found_via: WebSearch: fast pseudorandom number generator paper faster than xoshiro PCG Mersenne Twister github

name: AMGCL
workload: 3D Poisson problem, 3,375,000 unknowns, shared-memory AMG setup and solve versus PETSc and Trilinos ML.
claimed_speedup: AMGCL setup is 20-100% faster than Trilinos, and 4-7 times faster than PETSC; GPU solution phase 3-4 times faster than CPU versions
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon E5-2640 v3 (plus NVIDIA Tesla K80 for GPU runs)
tradeoffs: Header-only; AMG hierarchy built on CPU, solve phase on OpenMP/OpenCL/CUDA backends. Setup-phase advantage only; solve-phase comparison not claimed as faster.
caveats: First-party docs page; compiler flags not stated; hardware is old (Xeon E5 v3, Tesla K80). Distributed-memory runs show AMGCL about 3x worse than AMG-based Trilinos. PETSc/Trilinos configuration not given on the page.
found_via: GitHub: web search 'github sparse linear solver library faster than Eigen SimplicialLDLT benchmark C++' surfaced ddemidov/amgcl; benchmark page via docs link

name: ISpMV
workload: GPU SpMV (fp64, alpha/beta variants, A and A^T) over 49 Mittelmann, 18 MIPLIB and 33 SuiteSparse large matrices on H100 PCIe.
claimed_speedup: 2.17x (Mittelmann), 1.64x (MIPLIB nnz>10M), 1.31x (SuiteSparse nnz>10M) geometric-mean speedup over cuSPARSE for alpha=1,beta=0
license: MIT (interfaces, examples, benchmarks) plus proprietary ISpMV Binary License for compiled core
tradeoffs: Needs a one-time GPU preprocessing plan per matrix (37-110 ms geometric mean per direction); NVIDIA GPU only; core is a closed binary SDK.
caveats: Core is binary-licensed (not open source); compiler flags and CPU not stated; speedup values come from an LLM summary of the benchmark page, not verified row by row; baseline is cuSPARSE, not on the list. Mark low confidence.
found_via: GitHub: web search 'github sparse matrix-vector multiplication SpMV library faster than MKL Eigen SuiteSparse C++ benchmark'
